stops.name: Salta, the victory
stops.campa: She serves through Belgrano's second great victory, at Salta on 20 February 1813, where the royalist General Tristán's entire force is compelled to surrender in the field. Witnesses of the campaign recall her moving among the fallen with water and calling the chaplains to the dying, steady work she has by now done through three battles running. For a season it seems the war might actually be won; Remedios, Capitana, keeps doing the same unglamorous labor whichever way the day turns.

stops.name: Vilcapugio, the first defeat
stops.campa: On the high plateau of Vilcapugio, on 1 October 1813, Belgrano's army is winning the field against Pezuela's royalists until a broken order and a collapsing flank turn victory into rout within the hour. Remedios, who has followed this army through Huaqui, Tucumán and Salta, follows it now into its worst afternoon yet: the wounded piling up faster than she and the other women of the camp can carry water to them, the mountains around Vilcapugio closing on a beaten force.

stops.name: Ayohuma, water under fire
stops.campa: Six weeks later, on the llanos de Ayohuma, Belgrano's remade army meets Pezuela again. Remedios crosses the open field under cannon fire with a party of women the tradition will remember as las valientes mujeres de Ayohuma, carrying water to men collapsing from wounds and thirst alike; some of these women, the canon says, take up arms themselves when the royalist line closes in. It is the hour that earns Remedios and her companions their place in the country's memory, hours before the same battle turns entirely against them.

stops.name: Ayohuma, wounded and taken
stops.campa: As the Auxiliary Army breaks a second time in six weeks, a royalist ball finds Remedios on the field and she falls with it; Pezuela's men take her prisoner among the hundreds swept up that afternoon. Belgrano, the general who commissioned her captain, is himself in retreat toward Jujuy with what remains of his command. For the first time since she marched north in 1810, Remedios belongs, however briefly, to the other side of the war she has spent three years serving.

stops.name: Potosí, sentenced to the lash
stops.campa: Identified among the captives as la capitana of the rebel army, Remedios is singled out from the ordinary prisoners for exemplary punishment. Three royalist commanders sign the order between them, Joaquín de la Pezuela, Juan Ramírez Orozco and Miguel Tacón, deciding that a woman commissioned by the enemy general deserves a particular lesson before the whole country: she is condemned to public flogging, to be carried out not once but on nine successive days, a sentence meant to be seen as much as felt.

stops.name: The nine days of public flogging
stops.campa: For nine consecutive days she is whipped in public, the punishment repeated rather than concentrated so that the town can watch it happen nine separate times. When it is over her body carries marks that will still be counted, verified and entered into an official record fifteen years later: witnesses before the Buenos Aires legislature will speak of six further scars of bullet and saber besides, but it is the nine days themselves, more than any single wound, that the canon holds up as the measure of what was done to her.

stops.name: En capilla siete veces, and the officers she frees
stops.campa: Beyond the lash, the canon holds that she is condemned to death and reprieved seven times, puesta en capilla, the night a prisoner is made ready to die: seven times the sentence is set and seven times, for reasons the record does not give, it is stayed. Through this same captivity she works the opposite miracle for others, using whatever freedom of movement a nurse is allowed among the royalist camp to help patriot officers slip away, nursing them, in effect, toward escape rather than toward the grave.

stops.name: Her own escape
stops.campa: Eventually Remedios slips the royalist hold herself and crosses back into land the patriots still hold, arriving with nothing but the scars of the lash and the name Belgrano's army has already given her. No account records the exact route or the day; only that she comes out of Alto Perú alive a second time, having survived Huaqui's disaster, four pitched battles, capture, nine days of public whipping and seven nights readied for death, and that she is, within the year, already serving again.

stops.name: Salta, joining Güemes' gauchos
stops.campa: Back in patriot territory, Remedios does not go home to Buenos Aires; there is, in truth, no household left for her there. Instead she takes up with the frontier war Martín Miguel de Güemes is building out of Salta's own gauchos: horse-and-lance militia who hold the line of the Alto Perú frontier against repeated royalist invasions from the north, fighting a war of ambush and retreat across the same quebradas she has already crossed twice as a soldier's woman and once as a prisoner.

stops.name: With Arenales in the guerra gaucha
stops.campa: She serves also under Juan Antonio Álvarez de Arenales in the guerra gaucha, the irregular hit-and-run campaigning that keeps the Alto Perú frontier contested long after Buenos Aires's regular armies have failed twice to conquer it outright. It is unglamorous war compared to Tucumán and Salta, fought village by village and ambush by ambush around Tarija and the borderlands, and it is here, serving without the rank or the recognition Belgrano once gave her, that Remedios spends the years the official histories will later simply skip.

stops.name: The trail goes cold
stops.campa: As the frontier war grinds on and its irregular campaigns are recorded badly or not at all, Remedios disappears from the documentary trail for years. No pay-book, no muster, no parish register names her through this stretch; the woman who survived Huaqui, fought at Tucumán, Salta, Vilcapugio and Ayohuma, endured capture and nine days of the lash, and freed other prisoners from a royalist camp, simply is not written down, and will not be again until she is an old woman begging in Buenos Aires.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the rancho on the outskirts
stops.campa: By the early 1820s Remedios is back in Buenos Aires, though not in any way the city troubles to notice: an old woman living alone in a modest rancho among the quintas beyond the built city, with no pension, no military honor visible on her, and no household left of the husband and two sons the war took at Huaqui. The republic she helped deliver is a decade old and has, so far, no idea that the captain who served it is living at its edge.
